lesson.title: Counting What's Good: Gratitude and Subjective Well-Being
lesson.summary: Subjective well-being, a person's own evaluation of their life satisfaction and emotional balance, is one of positive psychology's central outcome measures, and gratitude is among its most consistently studied contributors.
lesson.body:
Psychologists, including researcher Ed Diener, who did much of the foundational work defining the concept, use the term subjective well-being to describe a combination of two things: life satisfaction, a cognitive judgment about how one's life is going overall, and affect balance, experiencing more positive emotion than negative emotion over time. This is different from momentary happiness. It is closer to an overall self-assessment of the general shape of a person's life, made by the person living it.

Gratitude, noticing and appreciating something good that was given rather than strictly earned or expected, is one of the most studied contributors to subjective well-being. A well-known study by psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, published in 2003, had participants keep a weekly journal. Some listed things they were grateful for, others listed daily hassles or neutral events. Participants in the gratitude condition reported higher well-being than those in the comparison groups, a finding that has been influential and often cited, though as with most single studies, exact effect sizes should not be treated as precise or as guaranteed to replicate identically in every population.

Another tested exercise is the gratitude letter or gratitude visit: writing a detailed letter of thanks to someone who had a meaningful positive impact and, when possible, delivering it in person. This was one of several positive psychology interventions studied by researchers including Seligman and colleagues, and it produced a measurable boost in happiness in the studies that tested it, though the durability of that boost, like much early positive psychology intervention research, has turned out to be more variable across studies than initial enthusiasm suggested, and this remains an area of ongoing research rather than settled fact.

Several mechanisms have been proposed for why gratitude helps. It redirects attention away from what is lacking and toward what is already present, which can shift the balance of positive to negative affect described above. It can also strengthen a person's sense of connection to other people, tying gratitude directly to relationships, one of the five elements of the PERMA model, and to the social support that research on resilience consistently identifies as protective.
